Yes. One paper explicitly argues that a single general-purpose atmospheric model can handle many tasks: WIND is presented as a single pre-trained foundation model that replaces specialized baselines across tasks without task-specific fine-tuning, covering probabilistic forecasting, spatial and temporal downscaling, reconstruction from sparse observations, dry air mass conservation, and exploration of extreme weather under perturbations [1]. Another paper similarly finds that scaling a general-purpose model is sufficient for state-of-the-art probabilistic medium-range forecasting, without tailored training recipes [4].

The papers differ in scope. WIND is the clearest evidence for one model serving various atmospheric science tasks within weather and climate modeling [1]. Other papers show narrower forms of reuse rather than a single model for many tasks: one pretrained atmospheric diffusion model is conditioned on heterogeneous observations for super-resolution without retraining [3], while another atmospheric foundation model is adapted to sea surface temperature forecasting by fine-tuning [9]. A review of Earth observation foundation models cautions that no single geospatial foundation model is universally best [6].
